Microwaves | Travel in straight lines (line of sight); need towers or satellites | Long-distance telephone links, satellite communication, mobile networks
Infrared | Very short range, line of sight, can't pass through walls | TV remotes, some short-range device links

Network devices
Device | What it does
Modem | Modulator-demodulator: converts digital signals from a computer into analog signals for telephone/cable lines and back again
Ethernet card (NIC) | Network Interface Card: connects a computer to a wired network; has a unique MAC address
RJ45 connector | 8-pin plug used at the end of Ethernet (twisted pair) cables
Repeater | Regenerates and amplifies weak signals so they can travel further (needed when cable length exceeds ~100 m)
Hub | Connects several devices; broadcasts incoming data to every port (not intelligent, causes traffic)
Switch | Connects devices in a LAN; sends data only to the intended device using MAC addresses (intelligent, efficient)
Router | Connects different networks (for example, a LAN to the internet) and chooses the best path for packets using IP addresses
Gateway | Connects networks that use different protocols; acts as the entry/exit point of a network and often includes firewall functions
Wi-Fi card | Wireless network adapter that lets a device join a Wi-Fi network

Exam tip: Hub = broadcasts to all; switch = sends to the right device; router = connects different networks; gateway = connects networks with different protocols.

Topologies and network types
Topology is the physical or logical arrangement of devices in a network.

Topology | Layout | Advantages | Disadvantages
Bus | All devices share one main cable (backbone) with terminators at both ends | Cheap, uses the least cable, easy to add devices | If the backbone fails the whole network fails; hard to find faults; slows down with many devices
Star | Every device connects to a central hub/switch | Easy to install and manage; one cable failure affects only one device; easy to find faults | Needs more cable; if the central device fails the whole network stops
Tree | Star networks connected to a bus backbone in a hierarchy | Easy to expand; suits large organisations with departments | If the backbone fails, segments are cut off; more cabling

Types of network by area:

Type | Coverage | Example
PAN (Personal Area Network) | About 10 m around a person | Phone connected to earbuds or a smartwatch by Bluetooth
LAN (Local Area Network) | A room, building or campus (up to ~1 km) | School computer lab, office network
MAN (Metropolitan Area Network) | A city (up to ~100 km) | Cable TV network, a city-wide bank network
WAN (Wide Area Network) | Countries and continents | The internet, a company's offices across countries

Case-study questions: how to answer
A 5-mark case study describes a campus with several blocks, the number of computers in each, and distances between them. Answer each part like this:

- Server location: the block with the most computers (most traffic stays local; the 80–20 rule).
- Cable layout: draw a star from the server block to every other block (or the shortest total cable length if asked).
- Repeater: wherever a cable run is longer than about 100 m.
- Hub/switch: in every block, to connect the computers inside it.
- Best wired medium between buildings on the same campus: optical fibre for long or high-speed links, twisted pair for short runs.
- Connecting to a distant office: the network becomes a WAN; suggest the internet, leased lines or satellite links.
- Video conferencing / calls over the internet: VoIP; protection from outside attacks: a firewall.

What is a protocol?
A network protocol is a set of rules that defines how data is formatted, sent, received and acknowledged. Devices from different companies can communicate only because they follow the same protocols.

Protocol | Full form | Used for
HTTP | HyperText Transfer Protocol | Transferring web pages from a web server to a browser
HTTPS | HTTP Secure | HTTP with encryption (SSL/TLS); used for banking, shopping, logins; shows a padlock in the browser
FTP | File Transfer Protocol | Uploading and downloading files between computers
SMTP | Simple Mail Transfer Protocol | Sending email from a client to a mail server and between servers
POP3 | Post Office Protocol version 3 | Receiving email: downloads messages to the device and usually deletes them from the server
TCP/IP | Transmission Control Protocol / Internet Protocol | The core rules of the internet: IP addresses and routes packets; TCP breaks data into packets, ensures they all arrive, and reassembles them in order
PPP | Point-to-Point Protocol | Direct connection between two devices, such as a computer and an ISP over a phone line
TELNET | Teletype Network | Logging in to a remote computer and running commands (text-based, not encrypted; SSH is the secure replacement)
VoIP | Voice over Internet Protocol | Making voice and video calls over the internet: WhatsApp calls, Zoom, Skype

Introduction to web services WWW (World Wide Web): a system of interlinked documents and resources (web pages) accessed over the internet using browsers. It was invented by Tim Berners-Lee in 1989–91. The internet is the network; the web is one service running on it (others are email, FTP and VoIP). HTML (HyperText Markup Language): the language used to create web pages. It uses predefined tags like `

`, `

`, `` to describe the structure and display of content. XML (eXtensible Markup Language): a markup language for storing and transporting data. Tags are user-defined (such as `Riya`), and the focus is on what the data *is*, not how it looks. HTML | XML Displays data | Stores and carries data Predefined tags | User-defined tags Not case-sensitive | Case-sensitive Some closing tags optional | Every tag must be closed Domain name: the human-friendly name of a website, such as `cbse.gov.in`. DNS (Domain Name System) translates domain names into IP addresses. The last part (`.com`, `.org`, `.in`, `.gov`) is the top-level domain. URL (Uniform Resource Locator): the full address of a resource on the web. In `https://www.example.com/notes/sql.html`: `https` is the protocol, `www.example.com` is the domain name, and `/notes/sql.html` is the path to the file. Website: a collection of related web pages under one domain. Web page: a single document. Web browser: software that fetches and displays web pages (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari). Web server: a computer/software that stores websites and sends pages when browsers request them (Apache, Nginx). Web hosting: a service that stores your website on a web server so it is available on the internet 24×7.

chapterTitle: Database concepts and the relational model
sectionTitle: Why do we need a database?
text:
Why do we need a database?
Storing data in separate files (the file system) causes problems: the same data repeated in many files (data redundancy), copies that don't match (data inconsistency), difficulty searching and sharing data, and poor security.

A database is an organised collection of related data. A DBMS (Database Management System) is software to create, store, retrieve and manage that data: MySQL, Oracle, MS Access, PostgreSQL, SQLite.

- Reduces redundancy and inconsistency
- Allows many users to share data at the same time
- Provides security with user permissions
- Makes searching and reporting easy with queries
- Supports backup and recovery

A school example. The office keeps a fees file, the library keeps a members file and the class teacher keeps a marks file. Riya's phone number is typed into all three (redundancy). When she changes her number, only the office file is updated, so now the files disagree (inconsistency). A database keeps one copy of her details that every department uses.

File system | Database (DBMS)
Same data repeated in many files | Data stored once and shared (less redundancy)
Copies can disagree | One copy, so data stays consistent
Each new search needs a new program | Any question is answered with a query (SQL)
Weak security: anyone with the file can read it | Users get permissions (read only, read/write)
Hard for many people to use at once | Many users can work at the same time
Backup and recovery done by hand | Built-in backup and recovery

Some words you need: data = raw facts (92, 'Riya'); information = processed, meaningful data ('Riya topped 12A'); record = all the data about one item (one student); field = one piece of data in a record (Marks).

2-mark question: 'Give two advantages of a DBMS over a file system.' Write: (1) it reduces data redundancy, so there is less repetition; (2) it keeps data consistent, because one copy is updated. Security, sharing and easy querying are also accepted.

chapterTitle: Database concepts and the relational model
text:
The relational data model
In the relational model, data is stored in tables called relations.

Table: STUDENT
+--------+--------+-------+-------+
| RollNo | Name   | Class | Marks |
+--------+--------+-------+-------+
|    101 | Riya   | 12A   |    92 |
|    102 | Arjun  | 12B   |    85 |
|    103 | Meera  | 12A   |    78 |
+--------+--------+-------+-------+

Term | Meaning | In the STUDENT table
Relation | A table | STUDENT
Attribute | A column (field) | RollNo, Name, Class, Marks
Tuple | A row (record) | (101, 'Riya', '12A', 92)
Domain | The set of allowed values for an attribute | Marks: 0–100; Class: valid sections
Degree | Number of attributes (columns) | 4
Cardinality | Number of tuples (rows) | 3

Memory trick: Degree goes Down the top (columns across the header); Cardinality Counts rows. When two tables are combined by a Cartesian product, degrees add and cardinalities multiply.

Properties of a relation (table):

- Every row is different: there are no duplicate tuples.
- The order of rows and the order of columns does not matter.
- Each cell holds one atomic value (not a list of values).
- Every column has a unique name and all its values come from the same domain.
- A missing or unknown value is shown as NULL.

Worked example. A table CLUB has 5 columns and 12 rows. What are its degree and cardinality? 3 rows are added and 1 column is removed. What are they now?

Start:          degree = 5 (columns), cardinality = 12 (rows)
After changes:  degree = 5 − 1 = 4, cardinality = 12 + 3 = 15

Worked example 2. Table A has degree 3 and cardinality 4; table B has degree 2 and cardinality 5. Their Cartesian product has degree 3 + 2 = 5 and cardinality 4 × 5 = 20.

Common mistake: Students mix up the two. Degree is about columns (attributes); cardinality is about rows (tuples). The header row is not counted in the cardinality.

chapterTitle: Database concepts and the relational model
text:
Keys
Key | Meaning | Example
Candidate key | Any attribute (or set of attributes) that can uniquely identify each row | RollNo, AadhaarNo, Email
Primary key | The candidate key chosen to identify rows; must be unique and NOT NULL; only one per table | RollNo
Alternate key | Candidate keys not chosen as the primary key | AadhaarNo, Email
Foreign key | An attribute in one table that refers to the primary key of another table; links tables and keeps data consistent (referential integrity) | StudentID in RESULT refers to RollNo in STUDENT

STUDENT(RollNo PK, Name, Class)
RESULT(ExamID, RollNo FK → STUDENT.RollNo, Subject, Marks)

A RESULT row can only use a RollNo that already exists in STUDENT.

A composite key is a primary key made of two or more columns, such as (RollNo, Subject) in a marks table.

Worked example. Look at this table and decide the keys.

Table: MEMBER
+-------+---------+------------------+------------+-------+
| AdmNo | Name    | Email            | Phone      | Class |
+-------+---------+------------------+------------+-------+
|  5001 | Riya    | riya@iis.ae      | 0501234567 | 12A   |
|  5002 | Arjun   | arjun@iis.ae     | 0559876543 | 12B   |
|  5003 | Riya    | riya.k@iis.ae    | 0524567890 | 12A   |
+-------+---------+------------------+------------+-------+

Column | Can it identify each row? | Why
AdmNo | Yes | Every student has a different admission number
Email | Yes | No two students share an email
Phone | Yes | Each student's number is different
Name | No | Two students are called Riya
Class | No | Many students are in the same class

- Candidate keys: AdmNo, Email, Phone
- Primary key: AdmNo (the one we choose: short, never changes, never NULL)
- Alternate keys: Email, Phone (candidate keys that were not chosen)

Foreign key in action. A FEES table stores AdmNo as a foreign key that refers to MEMBER(AdmNo). The DBMS will refuse a fee row with AdmNo 9999 because no such member exists. This rule is called referential integrity.

CREATE TABLE FEES (
    ReceiptNo INT PRIMARY KEY,
    AdmNo     INT,
    Amount    INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (AdmNo) REFERENCES MEMBER(AdmNo)
);

Exam tip: A primary key can never be NULL and never repeat. A foreign key can repeat (one student pays many fees) and its values must match the primary key of the other table.

SQL, DDL and DML
SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language for working with relational databases. MySQL is a popular free, open-source RDBMS that uses SQL. SQL keywords are not case-sensitive, but values inside quotes are compared as stored; every statement ends with a semicolon.

Category | Purpose | Commands
DDL (Data Definition Language) | Define or change the structure of the database | CREATE, ALTER, DROP
DML (Data Manipulation Language) | Work with the data in tables | INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SELECT

Rules for writing SQL: keywords can be in any case (`select` = `SELECT`); text and dates go in single quotes ('Riya', '2026-03-15); numbers have no quotes; each statement ends with ;; a comment starts with `--`.

Command | Type | What it does
CREATE DATABASE / USE / SHOW DATABASES / DROP DATABASE | DDL | Make, open, list or delete a database
CREATE TABLE / DESCRIBE / SHOW TABLES | DDL | Make a table, see its structure, list tables
ALTER TABLE | DDL | Add, modify or remove a column; add or remove the primary key
DROP TABLE | DDL | Delete a table with its structure
INSERT | DML | Add rows
UPDATE | DML | Change values in rows
DELETE | DML | Remove rows (structure stays)
SELECT | DML | Read rows (a query)

The sample table used in this chapter. Every query below is run on this STUDENT table, and the real output is shown under it. Aisha's marks are NULL (she was absent), which helps you see how NULL behaves.

RollNo | Name | Class | Gender | Marks | City
101 | Riya | 12A | F | 92 | Sharjah
102 | Arjun | 12B | M | 78 | Dubai
103 | Meera | 12A | F | 85 | Sharjah
104 | Kabir | 12B | M | 64 | Ajman
105 | Aisha | 12C | F | NULL | Dubai
106 | Rahul | 12A | M | 71 | Sharjah
107 | Fatima | 12C | F | 88 | Ajman

Data types and constraints
Data type | Stores | Notes
CHAR(n) | Fixed-length text of n characters | Shorter values are padded with spaces; fast for fixed sizes like PIN codes
VARCHAR(n) | Variable-length text, up to n characters | Uses only as much space as needed; best for names
INT | Whole numbers | 
FLOAT | Numbers with decimals | 
DATE | Dates in 'YYYY-MM-DD' format | '2026-03-15'

Constraints are rules applied to columns:

Constraint | Meaning
NOT NULL | The column must always have a value
UNIQUE | No two rows may have the same value (NULLs are allowed)
PRIMARY KEY | Unique and not null; identifies each row; one per table

CHAR vs VARCHAR with an example: in a `CHAR(10)` column, 'Riya' still uses 10 characters of space (padded with 6 spaces). In a `VARCHAR(10)` column it uses only 4 (plus a small length marker). Use CHAR for values that are always the same length (Class '12A', Gender 'F'), VARCHAR for names and addresses.

Feature | CHAR(n) | VARCHAR(n)
Length | Fixed | Variable
Space for 'Riya' in size 10 | 10 | 4
Speed | Slightly faster | Slightly slower
Best for | Codes of fixed length | Names, emails, addresses

Constraints at work. The table was created with `RollNo INT PRIMARY KEY` and `Name VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL`. Watch what MySQL does when a rule is broken:

INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES (101, 'Zara', '12B', 'F', 70, 'Dubai');
-- ERROR 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry '101' for key 'student.PRIMARY'

INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES (108, NULL, '12B', 'M', 70, 'Dubai');
-- ERROR 1048 (23000): Column 'Name' cannot be null

A UNIQUE column also rejects a repeated value, but unlike a primary key it accepts NULL, and a table can have many UNIQUE columns but only one primary key.

sectionTitle: Database commands: CREATE, USE, SHOW and DROP DATABASE
text:
Database commands: CREATE, USE, SHOW and DROP DATABASE
These are the database-level DDL commands: they create, open, list and remove whole databases, before any table exists inside them.

CREATE DATABASE school;
USE school;
SHOW DATABASES;
DROP DATABASE school;      -- deletes the whole database with all its tables

SHOW DATABASES; and SHOW TABLES; list names:

mysql> SHOW TABLES;
+------------------+
| Tables_in_school |
+------------------+
| dept             |
| emp              |
| student          |
+------------------+

USE does not list or delete anything - it simply tells MySQL which already-created database your next commands apply to, until you USE a different one.

sectionTitle: Table commands: CREATE TABLE, DESCRIBE, ALTER TABLE and DROP TABLE
text:
Table commands: CREATE TABLE, DESCRIBE, ALTER TABLE and DROP TABLE
Once a database is selected with USE, these commands create and manage the tables inside it.

CREATE TABLE STUDENT (
    RollNo INT PRIMARY KEY,
    Name   VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
    Class  CHAR(3),
    Marks  FLOAT,
    DOB    DATE,
    Email  VARCHAR(40) UNIQUE
);
DESCRIBE STUDENT;          -- or DESC STUDENT: shows the structure

DESCRIBE STUDENT; shows the structure (not the data):

Field | Type | Null | Key | Default | Extra
RollNo | int | NO | PRI | NULL | 
Name | varchar(20) | NO |  | NULL | 
Class | char(3) | YES |  | NULL | 
Gender | char(1) | YES |  | NULL | 
Marks | int | YES |  | NULL | 
City | varchar(20) | YES |  | NULL | 

ALTER TABLE … ADD adds a new column. Existing rows get NULL in it until you UPDATE them.

ALTER TABLE STUDENT ADD Phone VARCHAR(15);

RollNo | Name | Class | Gender | Marks | City | Phone
101 | Riya | 12A | F | 92 | Sharjah | NULL
102 | Arjun | 12B | M | 78 | Dubai | NULL
103 | Meera | 12A | F | 85 | Sharjah | NULL
… | … | … | … | … | … | …

ALTER TABLE … MODIFY changes the data type or size of an existing column (needed in the practical list).

ALTER TABLE STUDENT MODIFY Name VARCHAR(40);       -- make the column bigger
ALTER TABLE STUDENT MODIFY Marks FLOAT;            -- change the data type
ALTER TABLE STUDENT MODIFY City VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL;  -- add a NOT NULL rule

ALTER TABLE … DROP removes a column and all the data in it.

ALTER TABLE STUDENT DROP Phone;        -- the table is back to 6 columns (degree 6)

Removing and adding the primary key:

ALTER TABLE STUDENT DROP PRIMARY KEY;          -- RollNo is no longer the key
ALTER TABLE STUDENT ADD PRIMARY KEY (RollNo);  -- works only if RollNo has no duplicates or NULLs

DROP TABLE STUDENT;        -- deletes the table and its structure

Command | Removes | Table still exists?
DELETE FROM STUDENT; | All the rows (DML) | Yes, empty table
ALTER TABLE STUDENT DROP Marks; | One column | Yes, one column fewer
DROP TABLE STUDENT; | The table and its structure (DDL) | No
DROP DATABASE school; | The whole database with all its tables | No

Exam tip: 'Differentiate DELETE and DROP' is a favourite 2-mark question. DELETE is DML and removes rows; DROP is DDL and removes the whole table.

INSERT and DELETE commands
INSERT adds new rows; DELETE removes rows. Both are DML - the table's structure never changes.

INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES (101, 'Riya', '12A', 92, '2008-05-14', 'riya@x.com');
INSERT INTO STUDENT (RollNo, Name, Marks) VALUES (102, 'Arjun', 85);  -- other columns get NULL

DELETE FROM STUDENT WHERE Marks < 33;
DELETE FROM STUDENT;        -- deletes ALL rows; the table structure remains

INSERT in two ways. Without a column list you must give a value for every column in order. With a column list, the columns you leave out become NULL.

INSERT INTO STUDENT VALUES (108, 'Omar', '12B', 'M', 81, 'Dubai');
INSERT INTO STUDENT (RollNo, Name, Class) VALUES (109, 'Sneha', '12C');

RollNo | Name | Class | Gender | Marks | City
108 | Omar | 12B | M | 81 | Dubai
109 | Sneha | 12C | NULL | NULL | NULL

DELETE: removing rows.

DELETE FROM STUDENT WHERE RollNo IN (108, 109);   -- removes Omar and Sneha
DELETE FROM STUDENT WHERE Marks IS NULL;          -- would remove Aisha

Check yourself: Before you run UPDATE or DELETE, run a SELECT with the same WHERE first. The rows it shows are exactly the rows that will change.

UPDATE command
UPDATE changes values that are already stored in existing rows - it does not add or remove rows.

UPDATE STUDENT SET Marks = Marks + 5 WHERE Class = '12A';
UPDATE STUDENT SET Class = '12C', Marks = 80 WHERE RollNo = 102;

Danger: UPDATE or DELETE without WHERE affects every row. In the exam, always check whether a WHERE clause is needed.

UPDATE: before and after. Kabir and Rahul's marks were re-checked. Add 5 marks to every 12B student whose marks are below 70:

RollNo | Name | Class | Marks
102 | Arjun | 12B | 78
104 | Kabir | 12B | 64
108 | Omar | 12B | 81

UPDATE STUDENT SET Marks = Marks + 5 WHERE Class = '12B' AND Marks < 70;

RollNo | Name | Class | Marks
102 | Arjun | 12B | 78
104 | Kabir | 12B | 69
108 | Omar | 12B | 81

Only Kabir changed (64 → 69); MySQL reports `Query OK, 1 row affected`. To change two columns at once, separate them with a comma:

UPDATE STUDENT SET City = 'Abu Dhabi', Marks = 75 WHERE RollNo = 109;

sectionTitle: SELECT, operators, aliasing and DISTINCT clause
text:
SELECT, operators, aliasing and DISTINCT clause
SELECT * FROM STUDENT;                          -- all columns
SELECT Name, Marks FROM STUDENT;                -- chosen columns
SELECT Name, Marks * 0.7 AS Weighted FROM STUDENT;  -- arithmetic + alias
SELECT DISTINCT Class FROM STUDENT;             -- remove duplicate values

Operators in WHERE: mathematical (+ − * / %), relational (= <> != > < >= <=) and logical (AND, OR, NOT).

Each query below is run on the sample STUDENT table shown at the top of this chapter. Study the output under each one.

1. Choosing columns, aliases and arithmetic. `AS` gives a column a new heading (an alias); use quotes if the alias has a space.

SELECT Name, Marks FROM STUDENT WHERE Class = '12A';

Name | Marks
Riya | 92
Meera | 85
Rahul | 71

SELECT Name, Marks, Marks * 0.2 AS Internal FROM STUDENT WHERE Class = '12A';

Name | Marks | Internal
Riya | 92 | 18.4
Meera | 85 | 17.0
Rahul | 71 | 14.2

SELECT Name AS "Student Name", Marks + 5 AS "After Bonus" FROM STUDENT WHERE City = 'Ajman';
-- NULL + 5 would still be NULL

Student Name | After Bonus
Kabir | 69
Fatima | 93

2. DISTINCT removes repeated values.

SELECT City FROM STUDENT;
-- 7 rows, with repeats

City
Sharjah
Dubai
Sharjah
Ajman
Dubai
Sharjah
Ajman

SELECT DISTINCT City FROM STUDENT;
-- each city once

City
Sharjah
Dubai
Ajman

3. WHERE with relational operators (= <> != > < >= <=).

SELECT Name, Marks FROM STUDENT WHERE Marks > 80;

Name | Marks
Riya | 92
Meera | 85
Fatima | 88

SELECT Name, City FROM STUDENT WHERE City <> 'Sharjah';

Name | City
Arjun | Dubai
Kabir | Ajman
Aisha | Dubai
Fatima | Ajman

4. Logical operators AND, OR, NOT. AND needs both conditions true; OR needs at least one; NOT reverses a condition.

SELECT Name, Class, Marks FROM STUDENT WHERE Class = '12A' AND Marks >= 80;

Name | Class | Marks
Riya | 12A | 92
Meera | 12A | 85

SELECT Name, City FROM STUDENT WHERE City = 'Dubai' OR City = 'Ajman';

Name | City
Arjun | Dubai
Kabir | Ajman
Aisha | Dubai
Fatima | Ajman

SELECT Name, Gender FROM STUDENT WHERE NOT Gender = 'F';

Name | Gender
Arjun | M
Kabir | M
Rahul | M

sectionTitle: WHERE clause: IN, BETWEEN and ORDER BY
text:
WHERE clause: IN, BETWEEN and ORDER BY
SELECT * FROM STUDENT WHERE Class = '12A' AND Marks >= 80;
SELECT * FROM STUDENT WHERE Class IN ('12A', '12B');
SELECT * FROM STUDENT WHERE Marks BETWEEN 60 AND 80;   -- 60 and 80 INCLUDED
SELECT * FROM STUDENT WHERE Marks NOT BETWEEN 60 AND 80;
SELECT * FROM STUDENT ORDER BY Marks DESC, Name ASC;   -- ASC is default

5. IN and NOT IN are a short way to write many ORs.

SELECT Name, City FROM STUDENT WHERE City IN ('Dubai', 'Ajman');
-- same as the OR query above

Name | City
Arjun | Dubai
Kabir | Ajman
Aisha | Dubai
Fatima | Ajman

SELECT Name, Class FROM STUDENT WHERE Class NOT IN ('12A');

Name | Class
Arjun | 12B
Kabir | 12B
Aisha | 12C
Fatima | 12C

6. BETWEEN checks a range; both ends are included.

SELECT Name, Marks FROM STUDENT WHERE Marks BETWEEN 71 AND 88;
-- 71 and 88 are included

Name | Marks
Arjun | 78
Meera | 85
Rahul | 71
Fatima | 88

SELECT Name, Marks FROM STUDENT WHERE Marks NOT BETWEEN 71 AND 88;
-- Aisha (NULL) is in neither list

Name | Marks
Riya | 92
Kabir | 64

7. ORDER BY sorts the output. `ASC` (ascending, smallest first) is the default; `DESC` is descending. In MySQL, NULL comes first in ascending order and last in descending order.

SELECT Name, Marks FROM STUDENT ORDER BY Marks;
-- ascending (ASC is the default)

Name | Marks
Aisha | NULL
Kabir | 64
Rahul | 71
Arjun | 78
Meera | 85
Fatima | 88
Riya | 92

SELECT Name, Marks FROM STUDENT ORDER BY Marks DESC;
-- highest first

Name | Marks
Riya | 92
Fatima | 88
Meera | 85
Arjun | 78
Rahul | 71
Kabir | 64
Aisha | NULL

SELECT Name, City FROM STUDENT ORDER BY Name;

sectionTitle: NULL: IS NULL, IS NOT NULL and LIKE
text:
NULL: IS NULL, IS NOT NULL and LIKE
NULL means 'no value / unknown'. It is not zero or an empty string. Comparisons with `= NULL` never match; use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL.

SELECT Name FROM STUDENT WHERE Email IS NULL;
SELECT Name FROM STUDENT WHERE Email IS NOT NULL;

LIKE matches patterns: `%` = any number of characters (including none), `_` = exactly one character.

Pattern | Matches
'A%' | Starts with A
'%a' | Ends with a
'%an%' | Contains 'an'
'_r%' | Second letter is r
'____' | Exactly 4 characters

SELECT Name FROM STUDENT WHERE Name LIKE 'M%';
SELECT Name FROM STUDENT WHERE Name LIKE '_r%';

8. NULL: IS NULL and IS NOT NULL. `= NULL` never matches anything, because NULL means 'unknown'.

SELECT Name FROM STUDENT WHERE Marks IS NULL;

SELECT Name FROM STUDENT WHERE Marks = NULL;
-- wrong way: always gives an empty set

Output: Empty set (no rows match).

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM STUDENT WHERE Marks IS NOT NULL;

sectionTitle: Aggregate functions: MAX, MIN, AVG, SUM, COUNT
text:
Aggregate functions: MAX, MIN, AVG, SUM, COUNT
Function | Returns | Ignores NULL?
COUNT(*) | Number of rows | Counts all rows
COUNT(col) | Number of non-NULL values in col | Yes
SUM(col) | Total | Yes
AVG(col) | Average | Yes
MAX(col) / MIN(col) | Largest / smallest | Yes

SELECT COUNT(*), AVG(Marks), MAX(Marks) FROM STUDENT;
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT Class) FROM STUDENT;

Each function on its own (sample STUDENT table; Aisha's marks are NULL):

SELECT MAX(Marks) FROM STUDENT;
-- highest marks

MAX(Marks)
92

SELECT MIN(Marks) FROM STUDENT;
-- lowest marks; NULL is ignored, not treated as 0

MIN(Marks)
64

SELECT SUM(Marks) FROM STUDENT;
-- 92 + 78 + 85 + 64 + 71 + 88

SUM(Marks)
478

SELECT AVG(Marks) FROM STUDENT;
-- 478 ÷ 6, NOT ÷ 7, because NULL is skipped

AVG(Marks)
79.6667

SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(Marks), COUNT(DISTINCT City) FROM STUDENT;
-- all rows / non-NULL marks / different cities

COUNT(*) | COUNT(Marks) | COUNT(DISTINCT City)
7 | 6 | 3

MAX and MIN also work on text (alphabetical) and dates (earliest/latest):

SELECT MIN(Name), MAX(Name) FROM STUDENT;

MIN(Name) | MAX(Name)
Aisha | Riya

With WHERE: the rows are filtered first, then the function is calculated on what is left.

SELECT MAX(Marks), MIN(Marks), AVG(Marks) FROM STUDENT WHERE Gender = 'F';

MAX(Marks) | MIN(Marks) | AVG(Marks)
92 | 85 | 88.3333

SELECT COUNT(*) AS Total FROM STUDENT WHERE City = 'Sharjah';

Total
3

GROUP BY and HAVING clause
GROUP BY puts rows with the same value into groups so an aggregate is calculated for each group. HAVING filters groups (it can use aggregates); WHERE filters rows before grouping (it can't use aggregates).

SELECT Class, COUNT(*), AVG(Marks)
FROM STUDENT
WHERE Marks > 40
GROUP BY Class
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
ORDER BY AVG(Marks) DESC;

Order of clauses: SELECT → FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → ORDER BY. (Remember: Some Friends Will Give Help Often.)

GROUP BY: one result row per group. The rows are split into groups with the same value, and each aggregate is worked out for each group. (Without ORDER BY, MySQL may show the groups in a different order.)

SELECT Class, MIN(Marks), MAX(Marks), SUM(Marks), COUNT(*), AVG(Marks) FROM STUDENT GROUP BY Class;

Class | MIN(Marks) | MAX(Marks) | SUM(Marks) | COUNT(*) | AVG(Marks)
12A | 71 | 92 | 248 | 3 | 82.6667
12B | 64 | 78 | 142 | 2 | 71.0000
12C | 88 | 88 | 88 | 2 | 88.0000

See how 12C works: COUNT(*) is 2 (Aisha and Fatima are both rows) but the AVG is 88.0000, because only Fatima has marks.

SELECT City, COUNT(*) AS Students FROM STUDENT GROUP BY City;

City | Students
Ajman | 2
Dubai | 2
Sharjah | 3

SELECT Gender, AVG(Marks), MAX(Marks) FROM STUDENT GROUP BY Gender;

Gender | AVG(Marks) | MAX(Marks)
F | 88.3333 | 92
M | 71.0000 | 78

HAVING filters the groups after GROUP BY. It can use aggregate functions; WHERE cannot.

SELECT Class, COUNT(*) FROM STUDENT GROUP BY Class HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;

Class | COUNT(*)
12A | 3

SELECT Class, AVG(Marks) FROM STUDENT GROUP BY Class HAVING AVG(Marks) > 75;

Class | AVG(Marks)
12A | 82.6667
12C | 88.0000

All clauses together: WHERE removes Kabir (64) and Aisha (NULL), GROUP BY makes the groups, HAVING keeps groups with more than one row, ORDER BY sorts.

SELECT City, COUNT(*), MAX(Marks) FROM STUDENT WHERE Marks >= 70 GROUP BY City HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 ORDER BY MAX(Marks) DESC;

City | COUNT(*) | MAX(Marks)
Sharjah | 3 | 92

WHERE | HAVING
Filters rows | Filters groups
Works before GROUP BY | Works after GROUP BY
Cannot use MAX, SUM, COUNT … | Can use aggregate functions
WHERE Marks > 70 | HAVING AVG(Marks) > 70

Common errors:

SELECT Name FROM STUDENT WHERE Marks = MAX(Marks);
-- ERROR 1111 (HY000): Invalid use of group function
-- an aggregate cannot be used in WHERE; use HAVING, or a different query

SELECT Class, Name, COUNT(*) FROM STUDENT GROUP BY Class;
-- Error: Name is not in GROUP BY, so MySQL doesn't know which name to show

Rule: With GROUP BY, every column in the SELECT list must either be in the GROUP BY or be inside an aggregate function.

sectionTitle: Joins: Cartesian product on two tables
text:
Joins: Cartesian product on two tables
EMP(EmpID, Name, DeptID)          DEPT(DeptID, DName)
1, Asha, 10                        10, Sales
2, Ravi, 20                        20, IT
3, John, 10                        30, HR

Cartesian product (cross join): every row of the first table combined with every row of the second. Degree = 3 + 2 = 5 columns; cardinality = 3 × 3 = 9 rows.

SELECT * FROM EMP, DEPT;              -- 9 rows

Cartesian product: the full output. Every EMP row is joined to every DEPT row: degree 3 + 2 = 5, cardinality 3 × 3 = 9. Most rows are meaningless (Asha is not in IT *and* HR), which is why we add a join condition.

SELECT * FROM EMP, DEPT;
-- the row order may differ on your computer

EmpID | Name | DeptID | DeptID | DName
1 | Asha | 10 | 10 | Sales
1 | Asha | 10 | 20 | IT
1 | Asha | 10 | 30 | HR
2 | Ravi | 20 | 10 | Sales
2 | Ravi | 20 | 20 | IT
2 | Ravi | 20 | 30 | HR
3 | John | 10 | 10 | Sales
3 | John | 10 | 20 | IT
3 | John | 10 | 30 | HR

Most of these 9 rows are meaningless - Asha is not really in Sales, IT *and* HR at once. The next lesson (Equi-join) adds a condition so only the matching rows are kept.

Joins: Equi-join
EMP(EmpID, Name, DeptID)          DEPT(DeptID, DName)
1, Asha, 10                        10, Sales
2, Ravi, 20                        20, IT
3, John, 10                        30, HR

Equi-join: a join with an equality condition on the common column. The common column appears twice in `SELECT *`. Use `table.column` to avoid ambiguity, or table aliases.

SELECT Name, DName FROM EMP, DEPT WHERE EMP.DeptID = DEPT.DeptID;
SELECT E.Name, D.DName FROM EMP E, DEPT D WHERE E.DeptID = D.DeptID AND D.DName = 'Sales';
-- Asha Sales, John Sales

Equi-join (all columns). Only the matching rows are kept. With `SELECT *` the common column DeptID appears twice.

SELECT * FROM EMP, DEPT WHERE EMP.DeptID = DEPT.DeptID;

EmpID | Name | DeptID | DeptID | DName
1 | Asha | 10 | 10 | Sales
2 | Ravi | 20 | 20 | IT
3 | John | 10 | 10 | Sales

HR (30) is missing from the output because no employee is in department 30.

SELECT E.Name, D.DName FROM EMP E, DEPT D WHERE E.DeptID = D.DeptID ORDER BY E.Name;
-- E and D are table aliases

Name | DName
Asha | Sales
John | Sales
Ravi | IT

SELECT E.Name FROM EMP E, DEPT D WHERE E.DeptID = D.DeptID AND D.DName = 'Sales';
-- join condition AND an extra condition

Name
Asha
John

Join with GROUP BY: how many employees are in each department?

SELECT D.DName, COUNT(*) FROM EMP E, DEPT D WHERE E.DeptID = D.DeptID GROUP BY D.DName;

DName | COUNT(*)
IT | 1
Sales | 2

Ambiguous column error: DeptID is in both tables, so MySQL needs to know which one you mean.

SELECT Name, DeptID FROM EMP, DEPT WHERE EMP.DeptID = DEPT.DeptID;
-- ERROR 1052 (23000): Column 'DeptID' in field list is ambiguous
SELECT Name, EMP.DeptID FROM EMP, DEPT WHERE EMP.DeptID = DEPT.DeptID;   -- fixed

Joins: Natural join
EMP(EmpID, Name, DeptID)          DEPT(DeptID, DName)
1, Asha, 10                        10, Sales
2, Ravi, 20                        20, IT
3, John, 10                        30, HR

Natural join: joins on columns with the same name automatically and shows the common column only once.

SELECT * FROM EMP NATURAL JOIN DEPT;   -- columns: DeptID, EmpID, Name, DName

Natural join: joins on the column with the same name automatically; the common column is shown once, first.

SELECT * FROM EMP NATURAL JOIN DEPT;

DeptID | EmpID | Name | DName
10 | 1 | Asha | Sales
20 | 2 | Ravi | IT
10 | 3 | John | Sales

Join | Condition | Common column in SELECT * | Rows here
Cartesian product | None | Twice | 9
Equi-join | Written with = in WHERE | Twice | 3
Natural join | Automatic (same column name) | Once | 3

Exam tip: If two tables with degrees 4 and 3 and cardinalities 5 and 6 are joined by a Cartesian product, the result has degree 7 and cardinality 30. An equi-join can never have more rows than the Cartesian product.

Why connect Python with MySQL?
Real applications (school portals, shop billing, library systems) use Python for the user interface and logic, and MySQL to store the data. Python talks to MySQL through the mysql.connector library (install with `pip install mysql-connector-python`).

Steps: (1) import the library → (2) open a connection with `connect()` → (3) create a cursor → (4) execute queries → (5) `commit()` changes (for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) or fetch results (for SELECT) → (6) close the connection.

Python program                      MySQL server
─────────────                       ────────────
import mysql.connector
con = connect(...)   ── login ──▶   checks user and password
cur = con.cursor()
cur.execute(query)   ── SQL ────▶   runs the query
cur.fetchall()       ◀── rows ──    sends the result
con.commit()         ── save ───▶   makes changes permanent
con.close()

Check that the library is installed by typing `import mysql.connector` in the Python shell. No error means it is ready. A `ModuleNotFoundError` means you must install it with pip first.

import mysql.connector as m
con = m.connect(host='localhost', user='root', passwd='tiger', database='school')
if con.is_connected():
    print('Connected to MySQL')
con.close()

Key functions
Function / attribute | What it does
mysql.connector.connect(host, user, passwd, database) | Opens a connection and returns a connection object
con.is_connected() | True if the connection worked
con.cursor() | Creates a cursor object used to run queries and hold results
cur.execute(query) | Runs one SQL statement
con.commit() | Saves changes made by INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE permanently
cur.fetchone() | Returns the next row as a tuple, or None if no rows are left
cur.fetchall() | Returns all remaining rows as a list of tuples
cur.rowcount | Number of rows fetched so far, or affected by the last INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE
con.close() | Closes the connection

Which rows do the fetch functions return? Suppose `SELECT Name, Marks FROM STUDENT ORDER BY Marks DESC` gives 5 rows: Riya 92, Fatima 88, Meera 85, Arjun 78, Rahul 71.

Call (in this order) | Returns | rowcount after it
cur.fetchone() | ('Riya', 92) | 1
cur.fetchall() | [('Fatima', 88), ('Meera', 85), ('Arjun', 78), ('Rahul', 71)] (all the rows left) | 5
cur.fetchone() | None (nothing left) | 5

Remember: fetchone() gives a tuple; fetchall() gives a list of tuples of whatever rows are still left. Each fetch carries on from where the last one stopped, so fetchone() called after fetchall() has already read everything returns None.

Inserting, updating and deleting
import mysql.connector as m
con = m.connect(host='localhost', user='root', passwd='tiger', database='school')
cur = con.cursor()

roll = int(input('Roll: '))
name = input('Name: ')
marks = float(input('Marks: '))

# %s placeholders: values are passed separately as a tuple
q = 'INSERT INTO STUDENT (RollNo, Name, Marks) VALUES (%s, %s, %s)'
cur.execute(q, (roll, name, marks))
con.commit()
print(cur.rowcount, 'record inserted')
con.close()

# format() style, often seen in CBSE papers
q = "UPDATE STUDENT SET Marks = {} WHERE RollNo = {}".format(95, 101)
cur.execute(q)
con.commit()

cur.execute("DELETE FROM STUDENT WHERE Marks < {}".format(33))
con.commit()
print(cur.rowcount, 'rows deleted')

Don't forget: Without `con.commit()`, INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE changes are lost when the connection closes. SELECT queries don't need commit.

Style | Example | Note
%s placeholders | cur.execute('SELECT * FROM STUDENT WHERE Marks > %s', (80,)) | Values go in a tuple as the 2nd argument. Use %s for every type, even numbers
format() | cur.execute('SELECT * FROM STUDENT WHERE Marks > {}'.format(80)) | Text values need quotes inside the query: WHERE Name = '{}'

# A text value with format(): note the quotes around {}
name = 'Riya'
cur.execute("SELECT * FROM STUDENT WHERE Name = '{}'".format(name))

# One value with %s: the comma makes it a tuple
cur.execute('DELETE FROM STUDENT WHERE RollNo = %s', (105,))
con.commit()

Common mistakes: forgetting `con.commit()` (changes are lost); writing `(105)` instead of `(105,)` (not a tuple); forgetting the quotes around a text value with format().

Reading records
import mysql.connector as m
con = m.connect(host='localhost', user='root', passwd='tiger', database='school')
cur = con.cursor()
cur.execute('SELECT * FROM STUDENT WHERE Marks > 80')

rows = cur.fetchall()        # list of tuples
for r in rows:
    print(r[0], r[1], r[2])
print('Total:', cur.rowcount)
con.close()

cur.execute('SELECT Name, Marks FROM STUDENT ORDER BY Marks DESC')
top = cur.fetchone()            # first row only, e.g. ('Riya', 92.0)
rest = cur.fetchall()           # every row still left after fetchone()
print(top, rest, cur.rowcount)  # rowcount = 5 rows fetched so far

A complete menu-driven program (a common 5-mark question) combines these: show a menu (1. Add 2. Display 3. Search 4. Update 5. Delete 6. Exit) in a `while True` loop and call the matching query for each choice.

A complete menu-driven program (practise this one: it covers every function in the syllabus).

import mysql.connector as m
con = m.connect(host='localhost', user='root', passwd='tiger', database='school')
cur = con.cursor()

while True:
    print('1.Add  2.Show all  3.Search  4.Update marks  5.Delete  6.Exit')
    ch = input('Choice: ')
    if ch == '1':
        r = int(input('Roll: ')); n = input('Name: '); mk = int(input('Marks: '))
        cur.execute('INSERT INTO STUDENT (RollNo, Name, Marks) VALUES (%s, %s, %s)', (r, n, mk))
        con.commit()
        print(cur.rowcount, 'record added')
    elif ch == '2':
        cur.execute('SELECT RollNo, Name, Marks FROM STUDENT ORDER BY RollNo')
        for row in cur.fetchall():
            print(row)
        print('Total rows:', cur.rowcount)
    elif ch == '3':
        r = int(input('Roll to search: '))
        cur.execute('SELECT Name, Marks FROM STUDENT WHERE RollNo = %s', (r,))
        row = cur.fetchone()
        print(row if row else 'Not found')
    elif ch == '4':
        r = int(input('Roll: ')); mk = int(input('New marks: '))
        cur.execute('UPDATE STUDENT SET Marks = {} WHERE RollNo = {}'.format(mk, r))
        con.commit()
        print('Updated' if cur.rowcount else 'Roll not found')
    elif ch == '5':
        r = int(input('Roll to delete: '))
        cur.execute('DELETE FROM STUDENT WHERE RollNo = %s', (r,))
        con.commit()
        print(cur.rowcount, 'record deleted')
    elif ch == '6':
        break
con.close()

Sample run

Choice: 3
Roll to search: 103
('Meera', 85)
Choice: 4
Roll: 104
New marks: 70
Updated
Choice: 5

0 record deleted
